entities.name: Tiberius Pollienus Armenius Peregrinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tiberius Pollienus Armenius Peregrinus, a scion of the Roman senatorial aristocracy, achieved the esteemed office of *consul ordinarius* in 244 CE, sharing the fasces with Emperor Marcus Julius Philippus, known as Philip the Arab. His consulship occurred at the very outset of Philip's reign, immediately following the suspicious death of Emperor Gordian III, an event in which Philip himself was implicated. Peregrinus's elevation to this highest magistracy underscores the continued importance of senatorial legitimacy and traditional Roman institutions even amidst the profound political and military turbulence of the Crisis of the Third Century, a period characterized by frequent changes of emperor, barbarian incursions, and economic collapse. His career reflects the enduring, albeit diminished, influence of the old Roman nobility in an age increasingly dominated by military strongmen.

His tenure as consul in 244 CE was primarily ceremonial but symbolically crucial, affirming the continuity of Roman governance and the traditional hierarchy of power. The precise details of Peregrinus's administrative or military contributions beyond his consulship are largely unrecorded, a common fate for many senators whose public careers were overshadowed by the more dramatic exploits of the soldier-emperors. However, holding the consulship alongside the reigning emperor was a definitive mark of imperial favor and political prominence, suggesting he was a trusted figure within Philip's new administration. This period saw Philip the Arab negotiate a costly peace with the Sasanian Empire, which had been a major foreign policy challenge for Gordian III, and Peregrinus would have been part of the senatorial body ratifying such significant treaties and decrees.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tiberius Pollienus Armenius Peregrinus's consulship in 244 CE, though not marking a turning point, demonstrates the enduring symbolic power of traditional Roman institutions and the resilience of the senatorial class amidst profound imperial instability. His role underscores the attempts by new emperors to legitimize their rule through continuity with established Roman order.
